rows.speaker: عطاء
rows.claim: After the declaration that God is one, Quraysh asked how one deity could suffice all people; the verse was revealed in response.
rows.anchor: قال عطاء: لما نزلت { وإلهكم إله واحد } قالت كفار قريش

rows.speaker: أبو الضحى
rows.claim: A report through Sufyan says Quraysh asked for proof of the one God, and this verse supplied signs of divine unity.
rows.anchor: قالوا هل من دليل على ذلك؟ فأنزل الله تعالى { إن في خلق السماوات والأرض }

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The world's remarkable construction requires a builder and maker, so its order evidences God's oneness.
rows.anchor: فبين لهم دليل التوحيد، وأن هذا العالم والبناء العجيب لا بد له من بان وصانع

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The heavens are plural because they comprise differing kinds, while earth is singular because it is all soil.
rows.anchor: وجمع السموات لأنها أجناس مختلفة كل سماء من جنس غير جنس الأخرى. ووحد الأرض لأنها كلها تراب

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The heavens' height without supports below or attachments above manifests power and the breaking of ordinary patterns.
rows.anchor: ارتفاعها بغير عمد من تحتها ولا علائق من فوقها ودل ذلك على القدرة وخرق العادة

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: A prophet's stopping a mountain in the air without support would count as a miracle, by analogy with the unsupported heavens.
rows.anchor: ولو جاء نبي فتحدي بوقوف جبل في الهواء دون علاقة كان معجزا

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The sun, moon, moving stars, and bright planets, whether rising, setting, shining, or eclipsed, are further signs.
rows.anchor: ثم ما فيها من الشمس والقمر والنجوم السائرة والكواكب الزاهرة

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The earth's seas, rivers, minerals, trees, plains, and rugged places are signs of divine power.
rows.anchor: وآية الأرض: بحارها وأنهارها ومعادنها وشجرها وسهلها ووعرها

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Night and day differ by one arriving as the other departs in a way people do not know how to cause, or by light and darkness and changing lengths.
rows.anchor: اختلافهما بإقبال أحدهما وإدبار الآخر من حيث لا يعلم

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Layl has the collective plural layl as with tamra/tamr and nakhla/nakhl, and also the exceptional plurals layali and layal.
rows.anchor: والليل جمع ليلة مثل تمرة وتمر ونخلة ونخل. ويجمع أيضا ليالي وليال بمعنى

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Layali and similar plurals depart from regular patterns; the poetry cites laylat, and Ibn Faris reports an uncertain bird-name layl.
rows.anchor: وهو مما شذ عن قياس الجموع كشبه ومشابه وحاجة وحوائج

rows.speaker: ابن فارس
rows.claim: Ibn Faris says a certain bird is reportedly called layl, though he does not know the bird.
rows.anchor: قال ابن فارس في المجمل: ويقال إن بعض الطير يسمى ليلا ولا أعرفه

rows.speaker: أحمد بن يحيى ثعلب
rows.claim: Thalab treats nahr as a plural of nahar, itself a collective plural for day; another view treats nahar as a singular verbal noun meaning illumination, with the plural view more common.
rows.anchor: نهر جمع نهر وهو جمع الجمع للنهار

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The source cites poetry using laylat and nahr and notes nahar may be an unpluralized singular like diya, applying to little or much.
rows.anchor: وقيل النهار اسم مفرد لم يجمع لأنه بمعنى المصدر، كقولك الضياء، يقع على القليل والكثير

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: A poem about two kinds of tharid uses layl and nahr, illustrating the vocabulary for night and daytime.
rows.anchor: ثريد ليل وثريد بالنهر

rows.speaker: ابن فارس
rows.claim: Ibn Faris lists nahr and anhar as plurals of nahar and defines day as daylight from dawn to sunset.
rows.anchor: والنهار: ضياء ما بين طلوع الفجر إلى غروب الشمس

rows.speaker: النضر بن شميل
rows.claim: Al-Nadr says day begins at sunrise, excluding the time before it.
rows.anchor: أول النهار طلوع الشمس، ولا يعد ما قبل ذلك من النهار

rows.speaker: ثعلب
rows.claim: Thalab also says Arabs begin the day at sunrise and adduces Umayya ibn Abi al-Salt's sunrise poem.
rows.anchor: أوله عند العرب طلوع الشمس واستشهد بقول أمية بن أبي الصلت

rows.speaker: عدي بن زيد
rows.claim: Adi ibn Zayd's verse marks the sun as separating day from night, supporting a sunrise-to-sunset day.
rows.anchor: بين النهار وبين الليل قد فصلا

rows.speaker: الكسائي
rows.claim: Al-Kisa'i's poem likewise associates daytime with the sun's rising.
rows.anchor: إذا طلعت شمس النهار فإنها

rows.speaker: الزجاج
rows.claim: Al-Zajjaj defines the beginning of day as the sun's appearing.
rows.anchor: أول النهار ذرور الشمس

rows.speaker: ابن الأنباري
rows.claim: Ibn al-Anbari divides time into night from sunset to dawn, day from sunrise to sunset, and an interval shared by both from dawn to sunrise.
rows.anchor: وقسما جعله مشتركا بين النهار والليل وهو ما بين طلوع الفجر إلى طلوع الشمس

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Qurtubi holds that day runs from dawn to sunset, citing Ibn Faris and Adi ibn Hatim's report in Sahih Muslim, where the Prophet interprets the cords as night-darkness and day-whiteness.
rows.anchor: والصحيح أن النهار من طلوع الفجر إلى غروب الشمس كما رواه ابن فارس في المجمل

rows.speaker: عدي بن حاتم
rows.claim: Adi used white and black cords to distinguish day from night; the Prophet replied that his pillow was broad, meaning night-darkness and day-whiteness.
rows.anchor: إن وسادك لعريض إنما هو سواد الليل وبياض النهار

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: This dawn-based definition governs oaths: someone who swore not to speak by day breaks the oath by speaking before sunrise; the Prophet's wording decides the dispute.
rows.anchor: فمن حلف ألا يكلم فلانا نهارا فكلمه قبل طلوع الشمس حنث

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: A language-and-Sunna-based view takes day to begin once broad daylight appears; the passage cites a poem for this interpretation.
rows.anchor: وأما على ظاهر اللغة وأخذه من السنة فهو من وقت الإسفار إذا اتسع وقت النهار

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: A poem cited for the broad-daylight definition describes a hand breaking open an opening, with something visible beyond it.
rows.anchor: ملكت بها كفي فأنهرت فتقها يرى قائم من دونها ما وراءها

rows.speaker: حذيفة
rows.claim: A report from Hudhayfa, transmitted by al-Nasa'i, supports the broad-daylight view; fasting passages will return to the question.
rows.anchor: وقد جاء عن حذيفة ما يدل على هذا القول خرجه النسائي

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Fulk means ships; singular and plural share the form but differ in vocalization, and the dual fulkan shows a separate plural pattern.
rows.anchor: الفلك: السفن، وإفراده وجمعه بلفظ واحد، ويذكر ويؤنث

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The Qur'an uses fulk as masculine in 36:41 and feminine here, and as a plural in 10:22; it can denote one vessel or several.
rows.anchor: في الفلك المشحون

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Some derive fulk from rotation, as in the sky's orbit, a girl's rounded breast, and a spindle whorl; a ship is so named for turning easily in water.
rows.anchor: وأصله من الدوران، ومنه: فلك السماء التي تدور عليه النجوم

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The ship is a sign because God makes it run over water and remain afloat despite its weight.
rows.anchor: تسخير الله إياها حتى تجري على وجه الماء ووقوفها فوقه مع ثقلها

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Noah first built ships after Gabriel showed him how, as reported; Ibn al-Arabi likens the vessel to an inverted bird, water below and air above.
rows.anchor: السفينة طائر مقلوب والماء في أسفلها نظير الهواء في أعلاها قاله ابن العربي

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: This verse and comparable passages establish that sea travel is generally permissible for trade or worship, including pilgrimage and jihad.
rows.anchor: دليل على جواز ركوب البحر مطلقا لتجارة كان أو عبادة كالحج والجهاد

rows.speaker: أبو هريرة
rows.claim: The Prophet was asked about sea travel when water was scarce; this report and Anas's Umm Haram account support sailing for jihad by men and women.
rows.anchor: ومن السنة حديث أبي هريرة قال: جاء رجل إلى رسول الله صلى الله عليه وسلم فقال

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: If sailing for jihad is permitted, sailing for obligatory pilgrimage is even more warranted; the Anas report has variant attribution through Umm Haram.
rows.anchor: وإذا جاز ركوبه للجهاد فركوبه للحج المفترض أولى وأوجب

rows.speaker: عمر بن الخطاب
rows.claim: Umar ibn al-Khattab and Umar ibn Abd al-Aziz are reported to have prohibited sea travel, a view Qurtubi says Qur'an and Sunna refute.
rows.anchor: وروي عن عمر بن الخطاب وعمر بن عبد العزيز رضي الله عنهما المنع من ركوبه

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The prohibition reports can be read as caution against risking lives for worldly gain, not as a ban on fulfilling religious duties.
rows.anchor: محمول على الاحتياط وترك التغرير بالمهج في طلب الدنيا والاستكثار منها وأما في أداء الفرائض فلا

rows.speaker: ابن العربي
rows.claim: Ibn al-Arabi reasons that God placed people on opposite shores and divided benefits between them, so ships ease the necessary crossing of the sea.
rows.anchor: قسم المنافع بين الجهتين فلا يوصل إلى جلبها إلا بشق البحر لها فسهل الله سبيله بالفلك

rows.speaker: مالك
rows.claim: Malik disliked women sailing for pilgrimage and jihad; Basran associates explain this by small Hijazi ships, lack of privacy, crowding, and an available land route, unlike larger Basran ships.
rows.anchor: إنما كره ذلك مالك لأن السفن بالحجاز صغار، وأن النساء لا يقدرن على الاستتار عند الخلاء فيها

rows.speaker: أبو عمر
rows.claim: Abu Umar states the principle that pilgrimage is obligatory for any free adult who can reach it by a generally safe route, regardless of sex or sea versus land.
rows.anchor: والأصل أن الحج على كل من استطاع إليه سبيلا من الأحرار البالغين، نساء كانوا أو رجالا

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Qur'an, Sunna, and reason permit sailing for worship and trade, but a person unable to bear it or perform required prayer must not sail.
rows.anchor: فرب راكب يسهل عليه ذلك ولا يشق، وآخر يشق عليه ويضعف به

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Sailing is forbidden when the sea is storm-tossed or safety is generally unlikely; permission applies when survival is more likely.
rows.anchor: إن البحر إذا أرتج لم يجز ركوبه لأحد بوجه من الوجوه

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: What benefits people in ships includes trade and other needs that improve their circumstances; both merchants and recipients of goods benefit.
rows.anchor: أي بالذي ينفعهم من التجارات وسائر المآرب التي تصلح بها أحوالهم

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: In reply to a critic asking where spices are mentioned despite the Qur'an saying nothing is omitted, Qurtubi points to the phrase about what benefits people.
rows.anchor: فأين ذكر التوابل المصلحة للطعام من الملح والفلفل وغير ذلك؟ فقيل له في قوله

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Rain revives the world and brings forth plants and provision; God also stores some water underground for later use, as 23:18 says.
rows.anchor: الأمطار التي بها إنعاش العالم وإخراج النبات والأرزاق

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Batha means dispersed and spread, as in the phrase about scattered moths; dabbah covers all animals, including birds that walk on their legs.
rows.anchor: ودابة تجمع الحيوان كله وقد أخرج بعض الناس الطير، وهو مردود

rows.speaker: الأعشى
rows.claim: Al-A'sha's phrase about the step of desert pigeons illustrates that birds are included among creatures that move on foot.
rows.anchor: دبيب قطا البطحاء في كل منهل

rows.speaker: علقمة بن عبدة
rows.claim: Alqama ibn Abdah likewise uses dabib of birds, supporting their inclusion under dabbah.
rows.anchor: صواعقها لطيرهن دبيب

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Winds vary as barren or fertilizing, calm or stormy, destructive or helpful, hot or cold; they also differ in direction and are regulated to carry ships safely.
rows.anchor: إرسالها عقيما وملقحة، وصرا ونصرا وهلاكا، وحارة وباردة، ولينة وعاصفة

rows.speaker: أبو هريرة
rows.claim: The Prophet forbade cursing the wind because it brings mercy and punishment, and taught people to ask God for its good and seek refuge from its harm.
rows.anchor: الريح من روح الله تأتي بالرحمة وتأتي بالعذاب فإذا رأيتموها فلا تسبوها

rows.speaker: ابن ماجه
rows.claim: Ibn Majah transmits a version repeating the ban on cursing wind and the prayer for its good and protection from its evil.
rows.anchor: لا تسبوا الريح فإنها من روح الله تأتي بالرحمة والعذاب ولكن سلوا الله من خيرها

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: A variant calls wind the nafas of the Merciful; Qurtubi explains this as relief, refreshment, and release attributed to God as its maker.
rows.anchor: المعنى: أن الله تعالى جعل فيها التفريج والتنفيس والترويح

rows.speaker: ابن عباس
rows.claim: The Prophet said he was aided by the east wind and the people of Ad were destroyed by the west wind; Qurtubi links this to the wind at the Confederates.
rows.anchor: نصرت بالصبا وأهلكت عاد بالدبور

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Nafasa means to relieve distress, as in the cited hadith about God relieving a Muslim's distress and a poem about the east wind easing grief.
rows.anchor: أي فرج عنه. وقال الشاعر: كأن الصبا ريح إذا ما تنسمت

rows.speaker: ابن الأعرابي
rows.claim: Ibn al-A'rabi says nasim is the first breath of wind.
rows.anchor: النسيم أول هبوب الريح

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The root of rih is rawh, so the small plural is arwah; riyah is a larger plural for euphonic agreement, and Hafsa's codex reads arwah.
rows.anchor: وأصل الريح روح، ولهذا قيل في جمع القلة أرواح، ولا يقال: أرياح

rows.speaker: حمزة والكسائي
rows.claim: Hamza and al-Kisa'i read rih singular here and in several passages; the other named qira'a variants continue in the next segment.
rows.anchor: قرأ حمزة والكسائي «الريح» على الإفراد، وكذا في الأعراف والكهف وإبراهيم والنمل

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The seven readers agree on the plural reading in the phrase al-riyah mubashshirat.
rows.anchor: ولا خلاف بينهم في الرياح مبشرات

rows.speaker: أبو جعفر يزيد بن القعقاع
rows.claim: Abu Ja'far generally reads winds in the plural when the definite article is present, with two exceptions; without the article he uses the singular.
rows.anchor: يجمع الرياح إذا كان فيها ألف ولام في جميع القرآن سوى

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Singular reading can denote generic wind in both small and large amounts; plural can reflect winds arriving from different directions.
rows.anchor: فمن وجد الريح فلأنه اسم للجنس يدل على القليل والكثير. ومن جمع فلاختلاف الجهات

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Plural is commonly paired with mercy and singular with punishment, following the Qur'an's dominant pattern; Yunus 10:22 is an exception for a single steady ship-driving wind.
rows.anchor: فجاءت في القرآن مجموعة مع الرحمة مفردة مع العذاب إلا في يونس

rows.speaker: النبي صلى الله عليه وسلم
rows.claim: A report says the Prophet prayed for winds in the plural rather than a singular wind; Qurtubi explains mercy winds as gentle and broken up, punishment wind as compact and severe.
rows.anchor: اللهم اجعلها رياحا ولا تجعلها ريحا

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Wind is moving air; a wind from the qibla-facing side toward the qibla is called saba.
rows.anchor: قال العلماء الريح تحرك الهواء وقد يشتد ويضعف

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The four cardinal winds have distinct directions and temperaments: east hot-dry, west cold-moist, south hot-moist, and north cold-dry.
rows.anchor: فالصبا حارة يابسة، والدبور باردة رطبة، والجنوب حارة رطبة، والشمال باردة يابسة

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The four seasons follow these air qualities: spring is warm and moist for growth, summer hot and dry for ripening, autumn cold and dry for harvest, and winter cold and moist before spring renews growth.
rows.anchor: فجعل الربيع الذي هو أول الفصول حارا رطبا، ورتب فيه النشء والنمو

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Many other winds exist, but the four are foundational; a wind between two is called nakba and takes its ruling from the nearer direction.
rows.anchor: إلا أن الأصول هذه الأربع. فكل ريح تهب بين ريحين فحكمها حكم الريح

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Sahab is named for gliding through air; musakhkhar most plainly means moved from place to place, though another view says it stays suspended unsupported.
rows.anchor: والمسخر: المذلل وتسخيره بعثه من مكان إلى آخر

rows.speaker: أبو هريرة
rows.claim: The Prophet described a cloud directed to water a named man's garden; its water collected in a channel, and the gardener said he gave a third in charity, kept a third for family, and reinvested a third.
rows.anchor: اسق حديقة فلان فتنحى ذلك السحاب فأفرغ ماءه في حرة

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Qur'an 35:9 and 7:57 describe winds raising clouds and carrying them to a dead land, among many similar passages.
rows.anchor: والله الذي أرسل الرياح فتثير سحابا فسقناه إلى بلد ميت

rows.speaker: عائشة
rows.claim: When a threatening cloud approached, the Prophet sought refuge from its harm, prayed for beneficial rain if it rained, and praised God if it passed without rain; Ibn Majah transmits the account.
rows.anchor: فإن أمطر قال: «اللهم سيبا نافعا» مرتين أو ثلاثة

rows.speaker: عائشة
rows.claim: A Muslim report says the Prophet looked anxious in wind and cloud because he feared punishment for his community, then called rain mercy and recalled the people of Ad mistaking a cloud for rain.
rows.anchor: إني خشيت أن يكون عذابا سلط على أمتي

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: These reports and verses show that subduing clouds means moving them, not merely keeping them suspended; being between heaven and earth remains true, and their carriage is a greater sign.
rows.anchor: فهذه الأحاديث والآي تدل على صحة القول الأول وأن تسخيرها ليس ثبوتها

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Clouds are suspended and carried like birds; 16:79 and 67:19 say God alone holds birds in the sky.
rows.anchor: ألم يروا إلى الطير مسخرات في جو السمآء ما يمسكهن إلا الله

rows.speaker: كعب الأحبار
rows.claim: Ka'b al-Ahbar says clouds sieve rain, preventing it from damaging the earth; he also says seed descends from heaven, as transmitted through Ibn Abbas.
rows.anchor: السحاب غربال المطر، لولا السحاب حين ينزل الماء من السماء لأفسد ما يقع عليه من الأرض

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The listed phenomena are signs of God's unity and power, deliberately following the declaration that God is one and displaying mercy toward creation.
rows.anchor: ولذلك ذكر هذه الأمور عقيب قوله: { وإلهكم إله واحد } ليدل بها على صدق الخبر

rows.speaker: النبي صلى الله عليه وسلم
rows.claim: A prophetic warning says woe to someone who recites this verse and then fails to reflect or draw a lesson.
rows.anchor: ويل لمن قرأ هذه الآية فمج بها

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The world cannot create itself: a nonexistent thing cannot be living, knowing, powerful, and willing, while an existent thing needs no self-creation.
rows.anchor: فإن أحدثتها وهي معدومة كان محالا لأن الإحداث لا يتأتى إلا من حي عالم قادر مريد

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: If self-creation were possible, buildings, carpentry, and weaving could create themselves; since that is impossible, the implication is impossible.
rows.anchor: لجاز أن يحدث البناء نفسه وكذلك النجارة والنسج، وذلك محال

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Qur'an 10:101 addresses disbelievers, 7:185 calls them to inspect signs in the heavens and earth, and 51:21 directs them to examine themselves.
rows.anchor: قل انظروا ماذا في السماوات والأرض

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Reflection on change shows that the cosmos is originated and needs a maker; that maker must be wise, knowing, powerful, willing, hearing, seeing, and speaking, or a human would surpass him.
rows.anchor: وأن المحدث لا يستغني عن صانع يصنعه، وأن ذلك الصانع حكيم عالم قدير مريد سميع بصير متكلم

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Human development from drop to embryo and flesh, and from youth to old age, happens without self-direction; this proves a maker transfers people between states.
rows.anchor: كان نطفة ثم علقة ثم مضغة ثم لحما وعظما فيعلم أنه لم ينقل نفسه

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: A philosopher says each feature of the macrocosm has a counterpart in the human microcosm, connecting 95:4 with the call to inspect oneself in 51:21.
rows.anchor: إن كل شيء في العالم الكبير له نظير في العالم الصغير، الذي هو بدن الإنسان

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The senses correspond to the stars, hearing and sight to sun and moon; the body also contains analogues of earth, water, air, and fire.
rows.anchor: فحواس الإنسان أشرف من الكواكب المضيئة، والسمع والبصر منها بمنزلة الشمس والقمر

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Veins are rivers, the liver the springs feeding them, and the bladder a sea receiving the body's fluids.
rows.anchor: وعروقه بمنزلة الأنهار في الأرض، وكبده بمنزلة العيون التي تستمد منها الأنهار

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Bones resemble mountains, organs trees, and body hair the plants and grasses of the earth.
rows.anchor: وعظامه بمنزلة الجبال التي هي أوتاد الأرض. وأعضاؤه كالأشجار

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Humans can imitate animal sounds and movements, making the person a small world alongside the large world, both created by one maker.
rows.anchor: فهو العالم الصغير مع العالم الكبير مخلوق محدث لصانع واحد لا إله إلا هو

rows.speaker: مجاهد
rows.claim: Mujahid says God prescribed Ramadan fasting for every community.
rows.anchor: قال مجاهد: كتب الله عز وجل صوم شهر رمضان على كل أمة

rows.speaker: النقاش
rows.claim: A report attributed to Daghfal ibn Hanzala, al-Hasan al-Basri, and al-Suddi says later generations added days around the month until fasting reached fifty days and was moved to a solar season.
rows.anchor: وفي ذلك حديث عن دغفل بن حنظلة والحسن البصري والسدي

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Qurtubi tentatively links this history to disapproval of fasting the doubtful day and immediately joining six Shawwal days to Eid al-Fitr.
rows.anchor: ولهذا والله أعلم كره الآن صوم يوم الشك والستة من شوال بإثر يوم الفطر

rows.speaker: الشعبي
rows.claim: Al-Sha'bi says Christians originally had Ramadan fasting but transferred it to the solar season; he would break the fast on the doubtful day even if fasting all year.
rows.anchor: لو صمت السنة كلها لأفطرت يوم الشك

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: One view makes the comparison concern the original obligation of fasting on earlier communities, not its timing or manner.
rows.anchor: التشبيه راجع إلى أصل وجوبه على من تقدم، لا في الوقت والكيفية

rows.speaker: السدي وأبو العالية والربيع
rows.claim: Another view says earlier Christians, and early Muslims, could not eat, drink, or have sex after sleeping at night; 2:187 later abrogated that restriction.
rows.anchor: فإذا حان الإفطار فلا يفعل هذه الأشياء من نام

rows.speaker: معاذ بن جبل وعطاء
rows.claim: Muadh and Ata say the comparison concerns fasting itself, not its manner or number of days, which may differ.
rows.anchor: التشبيه واقع على الصوم لا على الصفة ولا على العدة وإن اختلف الصيامان

rows.speaker: ابن عباس
rows.claim: Ibn Abbas says Jews fasted three days and Ashura; Muslims first did likewise, then Ramadan replaced that practice.
rows.anchor: وهم اليهود في قول ابن عباس ثلاثة أيام ويوم عاشوراء

rows.speaker: معاذ بن جبل
rows.claim: Muadh says the initial three-day and Ashura fast was replaced by the numbered days, and those were then replaced by Ramadan.
rows.anchor: نسخ ذلك «بأيام معدودات» ثم نسخت الأيام برمضان

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: La'allakum tattaqun expresses hope addressed to people; taqwa here may mean weakened desire as less eating curbs appetite and sin, or simply avoidance of sins, or general piety.
rows.anchor: كلما قل الأكل ضعفت الشهوة، وكلما ضعفت الشهوة قلت المعاصي

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The word uhilla implies that intercourse had previously been prohibited at night and was then made lawful.
rows.anchor: لفظ «أحل» يقتضي أنه كان محرما قبل ذلك ثم نسخ

rows.speaker: أبو داود
rows.claim: Ibn Abi Layla reports from companions that a person who slept before eating after sunset could not eat until morning; Umar and an Ansari encountered the hardship before this verse came.
rows.anchor: وكان الرجل إذا أفطر فنام قبل أن يأكل لم يأكل حتى يصبح

rows.speaker: البراء بن عازب
rows.claim: Al-Bara says fasting companions who slept before iftar could not eat until the next evening; Qays ibn Sirma worked all day, fainted after missing food, and the verse brought relief.
rows.anchor: كان أصحاب محمد صلى الله عليه وسلم إذا كان الرجل صائما فحضر الإفطار فنام قبل أن يفطر

rows.speaker: البراء بن عازب
rows.claim: Al-Bara also says men refrained from wives throughout Ramadan but violated the rule, so the clause about God knowing their self-betrayal was revealed.
rows.anchor: كانوا لا يقربون النساء رمضان كله، وكان رجال يخونون أنفسهم

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Ikhtiyan and khiyanah both mean betrayal; a sinner betrays himself by bringing punishment upon himself, though the root originally concerns failure to fulfill a trust.
rows.anchor: يقال: خان واختان بمعنى من الخيانة

rows.speaker: عمر بن الخطاب
rows.claim: Al-Tabari's account says Umar had sex with his sleeping wife after a late visit to the Prophet, and Ka'b ibn Malik did likewise; Umar confessed and asked for a dispensation.
rows.anchor: فوجد امرأته قد نامت فأرادها فقالت له: قد نمت فقال لها: ما نمت، فوقع بها

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Al-Nahhas and Makki give a variant in which Umar slept, then had sex, informed the Prophet, and the self-betrayal clause was revealed.
rows.anchor: وأن عمر نام ثم وقع بامرأته، وأنه أتى النبي صلى الله عليه وسلم فأخبره بذلك

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Laylat al-siyam is an adverbial phrase, with laylah singular because it is a generic noun.
rows.anchor: «ليلة» نصب على الظرف، وهي اسم جنس فلذلك أفردت

rows.speaker: ابن عباس والسدي
rows.claim: Ibn Abbas and al-Suddi take rafath as a euphemism for intercourse; al-Zajjaj and al-Azhari say it broadly covers what a man desires from his wife, while Ibn Arfa specifies intercourse.
rows.anchor: والرفث: كناية عن الجماع لأن الله عز وجل كريم يكني

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Rafath can also mean explicit speech about intercourse or obscene speech; cited poetry uses the term in those senses.
rows.anchor: والرفث: التصريح بذكر الجماع والإعراب به

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The preposition ila after rafath is unusual; it is carried by analogy with ifda', meaning intimate contact, as in 4:21 and comparable constructions.
rows.anchor: ولكنه جيء به محمولا على الإفضاء الذي يراد به الملابسة

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Qur'anic words can inherit a neighboring word's syntax through shared meaning: rahim is used with bi in the sense of ra'uf, and the poet says hamaltu bihi in the sense of conceived.
rows.anchor: ولكنه لما وافقه في المعنى نزل منزلته في التعدية

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The clause wives are clothing is a subject and predicate; nun is doubled because hunna parallels the plural marker in masculine forms.
rows.anchor: { هن لباس لكم } ابتداء وخبر، وشددت النون من «هن»

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Al-Nabigha al-Ja'di's poem illustrates the clothing image through spouses' intimate bodily closeness.
rows.anchor: إذا ما الضجيع ثنى جيدها تداعت فكانت عليه لباسا

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Another explanation is that each spouse covers and protects the other from what is unlawful, or conceals their intimacy from people's eyes.
rows.anchor: فجائز أن يكون كل واحد منهما سترا لصاحبه عما لا يحل

rows.speaker: أبو عبيد
rows.claim: Abu Ubayd says a wife can be called one's clothing, bedding, or waist-wrap; in Umar's cited poem, izar means wife, though another view says self.
rows.anchor: يقال للمرأة هي لباسك وفراشك وإزارك

rows.speaker: الربيع
rows.claim: Al-Rabi says wives are beds and husbands are covers; Mujahid explains that spouses are a source of tranquility for one another.
rows.anchor: قال الربيع: هن فراش لكم، وأنتم لحاف لهن

rows.speaker: مجاهد
rows.claim: Mujahid glosses the clothing metaphor as mutual tranquility, with each spouse settling with the other.
rows.anchor: أي سكن لكم أي يسكن بعضكم إلى بعض

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Takhununa anfusakum can mean that some people assisted one another in prohibited sex or eating after sleep, like you kill yourselves can mean some kill others.
rows.anchor: يستأمر بعضكم بعضا في مواقعة المحضور من الجماع والأكل بعد النوم

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Alternatively, each person betrays himself because the harm of the betrayal returns to him.
rows.anchor: كل واحد منهم في نفسه بأنه يخونها وسماه خائنا لنفسه

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Taaba alaykum may mean accepting repentance or easing the rule, as in 73:20; the word can also designate a concession in 4:92 and 9:117.
rows.anchor: أحدهما: قبول التوبة من خيانتهم لأنفسهم. والآخر التخفيف عنهم بالرخصة والإباحة

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Afa ankum may mean pardon for sin or expanded ease; a prophetic saying calls the end of the prayer time God's pardon, meaning facilitation.
rows.anchor: يحتمل العفو من الذنب، ويحتمل التوسعة والتسهيل

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Qurtubi takes God's knowing as knowledge of their actual conduct, taaba as easing the rule afterward, and afa as making matters easy.
rows.anchor: فتاب عليكم» بعد ما وقع، أي خفف عنكم «وعفا» أي سهل

rows.speaker: ابن العربي
rows.claim: Ibn al-Arabi remarks that Umar's self-betrayal became a law and a relief for the community, reflecting the honor of divine care.
rows.anchor: خان نفسه عمر رضي الله عنه فجعلها الله تعالى شريعة

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Bashiruhunna is a euphemism for intercourse, now permitted; it is called direct contact because the two skins touch.
rows.anchor: كناية عن الجماع أي قد أحل لكم ما حرم عليكم

rows.speaker: ابن العربي
rows.claim: Ibn al-Arabi argues Umar's intercourse, rather than Qays's hunger, occasioned the verse: if Qays were central it would begin by permitting food.
rows.anchor: وهذا يدل على أن سبب الآية جماع عمر رضي الله عنه لا جوع قيس

rows.speaker: ابن عباس ومجاهد والحكم بن عيينة وعكرمة والحسن والسدي والربيع والضحاك
rows.claim: These authorities interpret what God prescribed as offspring, inferred from its placement after the permission for intercourse.
rows.anchor: معناه وابتغوا الولد يدل عليه أنه عقيب قوله: { فالآن باشروهن }

rows.speaker: ابن عباس
rows.claim: Ibn Abbas also interprets what God prescribed as the Qur'an; al-Zajjaj says to seek the Qur'an's permissions and commands.
rows.anchor: ما كتب الله لنا هو القرآن

rows.speaker: ابن عباس ومعاذ بن جبل
rows.claim: Another report from Ibn Abbas and Muadh interprets the phrase as seeking the Night of Decree.
rows.anchor: المعنى وابتغوا ليلة القدر

rows.speaker: قتادة
rows.claim: Qatada interprets it as seeking God's dispensation and expanded ease; Ibn Atiyya calls this a good interpretation.
rows.anchor: اطلبوا الرخصة والتوسعة قاله قتادة

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: A further view says the phrase means seeking what God has allotted of wives and slave women.
rows.anchor: من الإماء والزوجات

rows.speaker: الحسن البصري والحسن بن قرة
rows.claim: They read the word as wattabi'u, follow; Ibn Abbas allowed this reading, but Qurtubi prefers ibtaghu, seek.
rows.anchor: ورجح «ابتغوا» من الابتغاء

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The command to eat and drink answers Qays's hardship, while the earlier command to approach wives answers Umar; Qurtubi begins with Umar's more important case.
rows.anchor: هذا جواب نازلة قيس، والأول جواب عمر، وقد ابتدأ بنازلة عمر لأنه المهم

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The Prophet's report presents true dawn as the horizontal light spreading across the horizon, setting the endpoint for eating.
rows.anchor: لا يغرنكم من سحوركم أذان بلال ولا بياض الأفق المستطيل هكذا

rows.speaker: الجمهور
rows.claim: The majority identify dawn with whiteness spreading horizontally across the horizon, as the reports and common practice establish.
rows.anchor: ولا بياض الأفق المستطيل هكذا حتى يستطير هكذا

rows.speaker: سمرة بن جندب
rows.claim: The Prophet warned not to be deceived by Bilal's call or the false vertical whiteness; the true dawn spreads horizontally.
rows.anchor: لا يغرنكم من سحوركم أذان بلال ولا بياض الأفق المستطيل هكذا

rows.speaker: عبد الله بن مسعود
rows.claim: A report from Ibn Masud contrasts false dawn as a vertical gesture with true dawn indicated by fingers spread horizontally.
rows.anchor: إن الفجر ليس الذي يقول هكذا وجمع أصابعه ثم نكسها إلى الأرض

rows.speaker: عبد الرحمن بن عباس
rows.claim: A mursal report distinguishes two dawns: a wolf-tail-like vertical light neither permits nor forbids, while horizontal dawn permits prayer and forbids food.
rows.anchor: هما فجران فأما الذي كأنه ذنب السرحان فإنه لا يحل شيئا ولا يحرمه

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Another group says fasting begins only once dawn is visible in roads and homes; this is reported from Umar, Hudhayfa, Ibn Abbas, Talq, Ata, al-A'mash, and others.
rows.anchor: ذلك بعد طلوع الفجر وتبينه في الطرق والبيوت روي ذلك عن عمر وحذيفة وابن عباس

rows.speaker: مسروق
rows.claim: Masruq says the early Muslims counted dawn only once its light filled houses.
rows.anchor: لم يكن يعدون الفجر فجركم إنما كانوا يعدون الفجر الذي يملأ البيوت

rows.speaker: حذيفة
rows.claim: Hudhayfa says he ate suhur with the Prophet when it was effectively daytime though the sun had not risen.
rows.anchor: هو النهار إلا أن الشمس لم تطلع

rows.speaker: الدّارقطني
rows.claim: A report from Talq ibn Ali says one may eat until the red dawn appears; al-Daraqutni calls Qays ibn Talq weak, and Abu Dawud says only Yamama transmit it.
rows.anchor: قيس بن طلق ليس بالقوي

rows.speaker: الطبري
rows.claim: Al-Tabari explains the later-dawn view by defining day as sunrise to sunset, but Qurtubi says the Prophet's night-darkness/day-whiteness explanation and 2:184 decide the issue.
rows.anchor: وتفسير رسول الله صلى الله عليه وسلم ذلك بقوله

rows.speaker: عبد الله بن أبي بكر
rows.claim: A raised report from Hafsa says fasting is invalid without resolving to fast before dawn; Ibn Abi Bakr is described as trustworthy and of elevated transmission, while another version is Hafsa's own statement.
rows.anchor: من لم يجمع الصيام قبل الفجر فلا صيام له

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The two intention reports support the majority's dawn cutoff and require intention before dawn, contrary to Abu Hanifa; fasting is worship and requires intention, so post-dawn eating cannot be permitted.
rows.anchor: دليل على ما قاله الجمهور في الفجر، ومنع من الصيام دون نية قبل الفجر، خلافا لقول أبي حنيفة

rows.speaker: سهل بن سعد
rows.claim: Sahl says min al-fajr was added after people tied white and black threads and continued eating until they could distinguish them; they then understood the reference as daylight.
rows.anchor: ولم ينزل «من الفجر» وكان رجال إذا أرادوا الصوم ربط أحدهم في رجليه الخيط الأبيض والخيط الأسود

rows.speaker: عدي بن حاتم
rows.claim: Adi ibn Hatim took the white and black threads literally; the Prophet joked about his broad nape and explained that they mean night-darkness and day-whiteness.
rows.anchor: إنك لعريض القفا إن أبصرت الخيطين ثم قال لا بل هو سواد الليل وبياض النهار

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The dawn is called a thread because its spreading whiteness appears extended; khayt can denote color, and fajr comes from a root meaning to break open or flow out.
rows.anchor: وسمي الفجر خيطا لأن ما يبدو من البياض يرى ممتدا كالخيط

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Fajr names the first visible, spreading whiteness of morning from the sun's rising point, which Arabs called the white thread.
rows.anchor: وهو أول بياض النهار الظاهر المستطير في الأفق المنتشر

rows.speaker: أبو دواد الإيادي
rows.claim: Abu Dawad al-Iyadi's poem calls dawn's first light a bright thread, illustrating khayt.
rows.anchor: ولاح من الصبح خيط أنارا

rows.speaker: بشر بن أبي خازم أو عمرو بن معد يكرب
rows.claim: A verse attributed uncertainly to Bishr ibn Abi Khazim or Amr ibn Ma'd Yakrib calls dawn a split, another name for its appearance.
rows.anchor: كأن بياض لبته صديع

rows.speaker: الشماخ
rows.claim: Al-Shammakh likens dawn splitting the night to a parted head; other poetry uses phrases for the clarity and first signs of morning.
rows.anchor: أشق كمفرق الرأس الدهين

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: A poem speaks of arriving before dawn's break while the morning star remains hidden, illustrating inbilaq al-fajr.
rows.anchor: فوردت قبل انبلاج الفجر وابن ذكاء كامن في كفر

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Night is the time for eating, drinking, and sex, while day is for fasting; outside a traveler or sick person, daytime allows none of these.
rows.anchor: جعل الله جل ذكره الليل ظرفا للأكل والشرب والجماع، والنهار ظرفا للصيام

rows.speaker: مالك
rows.claim: Malik says anyone who deliberately breaks Ramadan by eating, drinking, or intercourse owes both a make-up fast and expiation.
rows.anchor: من أفطر في رمضان عامدا بأكل أو شرب أو جماع فعليه القضاء والكفارة

rows.speaker: الشعبي
rows.claim: Al-Sha'bi agrees with Malik that deliberate breaking by food, drink, or sex incurs expiation.
rows.anchor: وبهذا قال الشعبي

rows.speaker: الشافعي
rows.claim: Al-Shafi'i and others restrict expiation to intercourse, relying on Abu Hurayra's report that explicitly describes sex with one's wife during Ramadan.
rows.anchor: إن هذه الكفارة إنما تختص بمن أفطر بالجماع

rows.speaker: مالك
rows.claim: Malik, al-Awza'i, Ishaq, Abu Thawr, al-Tabari, Ibn al-Mundhir, and reports from Ata, al-Hasan, and al-Zuhri impose expiation for any deliberate fast-breaking because one report states it without restriction.
rows.anchor: وقد علق الكفارة على من أفطر مجردا عن القيود فلزم مطلقا

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Qurtubi rejects the claim that broad and intercourse-specific reports describe one event; their different wording indicates two distinct cases.
rows.anchor: بل هما قضيتان مختلفتان لأن مساقهما مختلف

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: By al-Shafi'i's own principle, not asking for details despite differing circumstances should imply a general ruling; al-Shafi'i also imposes discretionary punishment for violating Ramadan's sanctity.
rows.anchor: ترك الاستفصال مع تعارض الأحوال يدل على عموم الحكم

rows.speaker: مالك وأبو يوسف وأصحاب الرأي
rows.claim: These authorities require the wife who had sex with her husband in Ramadan to owe the same expiation as him.
rows.anchor: عليها مثل ما على الزوج

rows.speaker: الشافعي
rows.claim: Al-Shafi'i requires only one expiation, whether the wife consented or was coerced, because the Prophet answered with one and did not distinguish.
rows.anchor: ليس عليها إلا كفارة واحدة، وسواء طاوعته أو أكرهها

rows.speaker: أبو حنيفة
rows.claim: A report from Abu Hanifa says both owe expiation if she consented, but only the husband if he coerced her; Suhnun holds the same.
rows.anchor: إن طاوعته فعلى كل واحد منهما كفارة، وإن أكرهها فعليه كفارة واحدة

rows.speaker: مالك
rows.claim: Malik says the husband owes two expiations, which a group of his followers regard as the settled doctrine.
rows.anchor: عليه كفارتان وهو تحصيل مذهبه عند جماعة أصحابه

rows.speaker: الشافعي وأبو حنيفة وأصحابه وإسحق
rows.claim: They say a person who forgetfully has intercourse or eats while fasting owes neither make-up nor expiation.
rows.anchor: ليس عليه في الوجهين شيء، لا قضاء ولا كفارة

rows.speaker: مالك والليث والأوزاعي
rows.claim: They require make-up but no expiation for forgetful intercourse or eating; Ata is also reported to hold this, though another report from him requires expiation for sex.
rows.anchor: عليه القضاء ولا كفارة وروي مثل ذلك عن عطاء

rows.speaker: أهل الظاهر وابن الماجشون وأحمد بن حنبل
rows.claim: They require make-up and expiation even for forgetful intercourse, reasoning the expiation report does not distinguish forgetfulness from intention; Ibn al-Mundhir says nothing is due.
rows.anchor: سواء وطىء ناسيا أو عامدا فعليه القضاء والكفارة

rows.speaker: مالك والشافعي وأبو ثور وأصحاب الرأي
rows.claim: Qurtubi says that if forgetful eating leaves a complete fast intact, deliberate intercourse afterward requires make-up and expiation as if there had been no lapse.
rows.anchor: فعليه إذا جامع عامدا القضاء والكفارة والله أعلم كمن لم يفطر ناسيا

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Qurtubi's scholars argue that the obligatory fast must last a complete day, so forgetful eating leaves make-up due under the command to complete the fast.
rows.anchor: المطلوب منه صيام يوم تام لا يقع فيه خرم

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The Bukhari-Muslim wording commands continuing the fast but does not mention make-up, addressing freedom from blame and continuation.
rows.anchor: فلم يذكر قضاء ولا تعرض له، بل الذي تعرض له سقوط المؤاخذة

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Qurtubi endorses the majority view that forgetful eating or drinking does not invalidate the fast and requires no make-up, based on Abu Hurayra's report; al-Daraqutni grades its chain sound and its transmitters reliable.
rows.anchor: إذا أكل الصائم ناسيا أو شرب ناسيا فإنما هو رزق ساقه الله تعالى إليه

rows.speaker: أحمد بن حنبل
rows.claim: Ahmad says no make-up is due for forgetful eating, citing Abu Hurayra, and laughs at the claim that Malik required it.
rows.anchor: ليس عليه شيء على حديث أبي هريرة

rows.speaker: ابن المنذر
rows.claim: Ibn al-Mundhir reads the Prophet's command to complete the fast as proof it remains entirely valid, with no make-up mentioned.
rows.anchor: وإذا قال «يتم صومه» فأتمه فهو صوم تام كامل

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Qurtubi reasons that deliberate intercourse afterward still requires make-up and expiation, as if the forgetful person had not broken the fast.
rows.anchor: فعليه إذا جامع عامدا القضاء والكفارة والله أعلم كمن لم يفطر ناسيا

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Qurtubi's scholars infer make-up from the requirement of a complete day's fast in 2:187; they suggest the no-make-up hadith may concern voluntary fasting, while Bukhari and Muslim's version orders completion without discussing make-up.
rows.anchor: المطلوب منه صيام يوم تام لا يقع فيه خرم لقوله تعالى: { ثم أتموا الصيام إلى الليل }

rows.speaker: أبو هريرة
rows.claim: An explicit report says whoever breaks Ramadan by forgetfulness owes neither make-up nor expiation; al-Daraqutni says only trustworthy Ibn Marzuq transmits it from al-Ansari, resolving the ambiguity.
rows.anchor: تفرد به ابن مرزوق وهو ثقة عن الأنصاري فزال الاحتمال

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The verse names eating, drinking, and intercourse as nighttime permissions but does not mention touching; therefore it alone does not prohibit kissing or touching during a fast.
rows.anchor: ولم يذكر المباشرة التي هي اتصال البشرة بالبشرة كالقبلة والجسة وغيرها

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Maliki scholars discourage touching for someone unable to control himself, to prevent it leading to a fast-breaking act; Ibn Umar prohibited kissing and touching for this reason.
rows.anchor: يكره لمن لا يأمن على نفسه ولا يملكها لئلا يكون سببا إلى ما يفسد الصوم

rows.speaker: عائشة
rows.claim: Aisha reports that the Prophet kissed and touched his wives while fasting, rebutting those who categorically prohibit it.
rows.anchor: كان النبي صلى الله عليه وسلم يقبل ويباشر وهو صائم

rows.speaker: عبد الله بن مسعود
rows.claim: Ibn Masud and Urwa disliked kissing; a report says Ibn Masud required make-up, but the Prophetic report is evidence against them.
rows.anchor: وممن كره القبلة للصائم عبد الله بن مسعود وعروة ابن الزبير

rows.speaker: أبو عمر
rows.claim: Abu Umar knows no one who permits kissing for someone who expects it to produce a fast-breaking result; ejaculation requires make-up but no expiation according to several jurists.
rows.anchor: ولا أعلم أحدا رخص فيها لمن يعلم أنه يتولد عليه منها ما يفسد صومه

rows.speaker: أحمد
rows.claim: Ahmad requires make-up if kissing causes preseminal fluid or semen, but expiation only for intercourse with penetration, whether deliberate or forgetful.
rows.anchor: من قبل فأمذى أو أمنى فعليه القضاء ولا كفارة عليه إلا على من جامع

rows.speaker: ابن القاسم
rows.claim: Ibn al-Qasim reports Malik requiring make-up after an erection with no emission; Ibn Wahb reports no make-up until preseminal fluid appears, and the school agrees there is no expiation.
rows.anchor: فيمن قبل أو باشر فأنعظ ولم يخرج منه ماء جملة عليه القضاء

rows.speaker: أشهب وسحنون
rows.claim: Ashhab and Sahnun require no expiation for one kiss or touch causing ejaculation, but require it if repeated; Ibn al-Qasim requires it in all such cases except looking without repetition.
rows.anchor: لا كفارة عليه حتى يكرر

rows.speaker: الحسن البصري وعطاء وابن المبارك وأبو ثور وإسحق
rows.claim: These authorities, and Malik in al-Mudawwana, require expiation for ejaculation caused by kissing, touching, play, or sex without penetration.
rows.anchor: وممن قال بوجوب الكفارة عليه إذا قبل أو باشر أو لاعب امرأته

rows.speaker: أشهب
rows.claim: Ashhab reasons one kiss is not itself invalidating and does not show intent to spill semen, while repetition indicates intent to violate the fast; repeated looking is analogous.
rows.anchor: إذا فعل مرة واحدة لم يقصد الإنزال وإفساد الصوم فلا كفارة عليه

rows.speaker: اللخمي
rows.claim: Al-Lakhmi says jurists agree that ejaculation caused by looking alone entails no expiation unless the gaze is repeated.
rows.anchor: واتفق جميعهم في الإنزال عن النظر أن لا كفارة عليه إلا أن يتابع

rows.speaker: اللخمي
rows.claim: Al-Lakhmi's principle is that expiation requires intent to break the fast's sanctity; habits and the likelihood of emission distinguish intent or recklessness from an unusual accident.
rows.anchor: والأصل أنه لا تجب الكفارة إلا على من قصد الفطر وانتهاك حرمة الصوم

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Qurtubi explains Malik's stricter view by habitual susceptibility and Ashhab's leniency by the common expectation of safety; their view on looking illustrates the distinction.
rows.anchor: وحمل أشهب الأمر على الغالب من الناس أنهم يسلمون من ذلك

rows.speaker: أبو الحسن
rows.claim: Qurtubi rejects a claimed consensus that one look never incurs expiation: Abu al-Hasan says one lustful look leading to ejaculation requires make-up and expiation, and al-Baji calls that correct.
rows.anchor: فإن نظر نظرة واحدة يقصد بها اللذة فأنزل فقد قال الشيخ أبو الحسن

rows.speaker: جابر بن زيد والثوري والشافعي وأبو ثور وأصحاب الرأي
rows.claim: These authorities say repeated looking that leads to ejaculation entails neither make-up nor expiation, as reported by Ibn al-Mundhir.
rows.anchor: فيمن ردد النظر إلى المرأة حتى أمنى: فلا قضاء عليه ولا كفارة

rows.speaker: مالك
rows.claim: Ibn Nafi reports Malik requiring make-up but not expiation if a man looks at an unclothed woman with desire and ejaculates.
rows.anchor: إن نظر إلى امرأة متجردة فالتذ فأنزل عليه القضاء دون الكفارة

rows.speaker: الجمهور
rows.claim: The majority say a person who enters dawn in major ritual impurity may fast; Ibn al-Arabi calls this settled consensus after earlier disagreement.
rows.anchor: والجمهور من العلماء على صحة صوم من طلع عليه الفجر وهو جنب

rows.speaker: أبو هريرة
rows.claim: Abu Hurayra is reported to have said that one who wakes junub has no valid fast, a position with differing reports about whether he later retracted.
rows.anchor: من أصبح جنبا فلا صوم له

rows.speaker: أبو هريرة
rows.claim: A third view attributed to Abu Hurayra distinguishes knowingly sleeping through dawn while junub from not knowing; Ata, Tawus, and Urwa transmit it.
rows.anchor: إذا علم بجنابته ثم نام حتى يصبح فهو مفطر

rows.speaker: الحسن والنخعي
rows.claim: Al-Hasan and al-Nakha'i say such a fast counts voluntarily but must be made up if obligatory.
rows.anchor: يجزي في التطوع ويقضي في الفرض

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Qurtubi prefers the majority on the strength of Aisha and Umm Salama's reports that the Prophet entered Ramadan dawn junub after intercourse, then bathed and fasted.
rows.anchor: كان يصبح جنبا من جماع غير احتلام ثم يصوم

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The permission for intercourse until dawn necessarily allows dawn to arrive while a person is junub, since ritual bathing can occur afterward.
rows.anchor: لما مد إباحة الجماع إلى طلوع الفجر فبالضرورة يعلم أن الفجر يطلع عليه وهو جنب

rows.speaker: الشافعي
rows.claim: Al-Shafi'i says that if a man withdraws from his wife as dawn begins, no make-up is due; al-Muzani disagrees because withdrawal completes intercourse, but Qurtubi favors al-Shafi'i.
rows.anchor: ولو كان الذكر داخل المرأة فنزعه مع طلوع الفجر أنه لا قضاء عليه

rows.speaker: الجمهور
rows.claim: The majority require and validate fasting for a menstruating woman who becomes pure before dawn but delays bathing until after it, whether deliberate or forgetful; Malik and Ibn al-Qasim agree.
rows.anchor: فجمهورهم على وجوب الصوم عليها وإجزائه، سواء تركته عمدا أو سهوا كالجنب
